title: Why does a sigmoid squash any number into 0 to 1?
story:
When building models that make binary choices, we often need to turn any real number into a probability between zero and one. Linear functions fail here because they grow without bound as inputs increase or decrease. We need a smooth, S-shaped curve that compresses extreme values while keeping moderate values sensitive to change.

Pierre François Verhulst faced a similar problem studying population growth, leading him to the logistic function. By dividing one by one plus the exponential of the negative input, the curve gently approaches zero for large negative inputs and one for large positive inputs. The steepness parameter dictates how sharply the transition occurs around the midpoint.

Exploring this curve reveals how nonlinear scaling maps infinite domains into bounded intervals. By adjusting the steepness, midpoint, and marker position, we can inspect the exact output and slope at any point along the sigmoid transition.
cardDescription: Explore how the logistic function maps any real number into the range between 0 and 1. Adjust steepness, midpoint, and marker position to inspect the curve and its slope.
instructions: Adjust the sliders to change steepness, midpoint, and marker position. Observe how the output stays strictly between 0 and 1.
learningGoal: Distinguish a shift of the transition from a change in sensitivity, using the marker and tangent.

scene.description: A curve with its formula in the heading, a tangent and the same legend/readouts. Three sliders change steepness, midpoint and marker input.

entities.label: Sigmoid curve
entities.purpose: Show output as a function of input.

entities.label: Selected point
entities.purpose: Link an input coordinate to its output.

entities.label: Local tangent
entities.purpose: Show the slope at the selected input.

quantities.label: Steepness k
quantities.reference: At x0 the slope is k / 4.

quantities.label: Midpoint x₀
quantities.meaning: Input at the centre of the transition.
quantities.reference: The output at x0 is one half. Increasing x0 shifts the curve right.

quantities.label: Marker x
quantities.meaning: Input coordinate of the selected point on the curve.
quantities.reference: The marker readout is y evaluated at this input.

quantities.label: Output y
quantities.meaning: Dimensionless output at x; strictly between zero and one for finite inputs. Positive is upward.

quantities.label: Slope dy/dx
quantities.meaning: Signed derivative of y with respect to x. Positive means the curve rises to the right.
quantities.reference: slope = k / (2 + exp(k * (x - x0)) + exp(-k * (x - x0)))

quantities.label: Output y
quantities.meaning: Dimensionless output at the selected input xMarker; the same curve, not a second rule.

observations.text: The output approaches either bound without reaching it at a finite input.
The tangent slope measures sensitivity at the marker.

checkpoints.label: Default curve
checkpoints.expected: The marker lies on the curve and its readout is the output at the marked input.

checkpoints.label: Least steep
checkpoints.expected: The transition is gentler; its output stays within the same bounds.

checkpoints.label: Most steep
checkpoints.expected: The transition is sharper around its midpoint; its output stays within the same bounds.

checkpoints.label: Midpoint at marked input
checkpoints.expected: The tangent and output change together at the selected input.

checkpoints.label: Left edge
checkpoints.expected: The marker reaches the left end of its admitted input range.

checkpoints.label: Right edge
checkpoints.expected: The marker reaches the right end of its admitted input range.

assumptions: Dimensionless logistic with positive steepness; a finite displayed input domain.
limitations: The plot shows a finite input interval; its bounds describe the full logistic.

claims.text: The output is strictly between zero and one for finite inputs with positive steepness.
claims.check: exp(z) > 0, hence 1 + exp(z) > 1 and its reciprocal is strictly between zero and one.
